assumptions.summary: Ideal single-species growth under sufficient resources, no drought, and no interaction follows the Logistic curve.
The modeled pairwise relationship set is restricted to competition and mutual benefit.
Drought stress is represented only by precipitation and excludes other hydrological or physiological drivers.
Environmental drivers other than drought, pollution, and habitat loss are omitted.
Plant response is reduced to sensitive and drought-tolerant classes, although the body later adds a standard class.
Extreme drought and flood lie outside the intended model domain.
Interaction index and carrying capacity respond linearly to drought-stress deviation around S0.
Growth rate follows a bounded Logistic-shaped precipitation response shared in form across species.
Fixed species biomass weights convert abundance trajectories to community biomass.
Root-shoot information can support directed K_sigma and S0 matrices.
Drought and pollution degrees are additively compatible, purification is linear, and capacity scales with remaining habitat.
A one-month fixed step and forcing held across stages make the printed first-order and RK4 simulations meaningful.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: The official problem supplies qualitative observations about richness and drought adaptability but no numeric plant-community dataset.
A 48-month average monthly precipitation series for 2018-2021 is attributed to the National Bureau of Statistics without station, unit, or table identifier.
Four Tengger Desert shrubs are renamed A-D and initialized at 34, 34, 29, and 33 plants, but observation area and date are not stated.
Ideal capacities 200, 153, 137, and 36 are assigned proportionally from qualitative drought adaptability.
Growth ceilings 5, 3.5, 5, and 2.5 plants per month are estimated from root length.
Table 2 assigns alpha=0.6, S0=0.5, k_sigma=0.002, and k_i=0.01 through unspecified fitting and empirical analysis.
Eq.9-Eq.10 provide 32 directed off-diagonal parameter entries attributed generally to root-shoot information.
Table 3 adds biomass weights 371.49, 156.32, 230.66, and 178.71 with no unit or exact source mapping.
The weather generator estimates 24 five-unit precipitation bins from only 48 monthly observations.
Listing 2 depends on the unshipped spreadsheet T and rainfall.xlsx, sheet2 E2:E49.
Greater- and lesser-drought scenarios are single 60-month random sequences produced by hand-edited marginal bin weights.
Table 12 introduces a stylized month-25 construction schedule with H=1,0.9,0.8,0.7 and pollution increment in [0.02,0.06].
Sensitivity uses the mixed-type scenario, four species, Li/Ni0/ki, and perturbations -10,-5,+5,+10 percent.
The appendix prints partial MATLAB code but omits input files, complete scripts, functions, seeds, environment versions, and output parity artifacts.

Eq.3-Eq.6 provide sigma_ij, r_i, and N_i to the multi-species population derivative.

Subset abundance trajectories are multiplied by B_i and compared with the Eq.7 monoculture envelope.
Directed K_sigma and S0 entries parameterize Eq.3 for the benefit experiments.
The beta_i type multiplier changes N_i before the same population system is simulated.
Generated monthly precipitation is converted to S and then drives the three environmental pathways.
Composite stress T replaces S while H scales capacity in the pollution-habitat extension.
Eq.12-Eq.15 supply the PO, T, and H quantities implemented by Listing 4.
The same population derivative is evaluated at four intermediate RK4 states.
RK4 abundance trajectories can be consumed by the existing biomass-benefit calculation.
The core model is rerun after local perturbations to Li, Ni0, or ki.

independent_extensions.summary: Calibrate precipitation, soil moisture or evapotranspiration, abundance, biomass, and interaction coefficients with one explicit spatial and temporal observation unit.
Replace the universal drought-driven sign switch with candidate interaction-response functions and compare them using data and uncertainty.
Define a feasible fixed monoculture comparator or a decision-specific biodiversity benefit metric with an explicit time aggregation and uncertainty interval.
Use controlled richness experiments that hold total initial abundance, species identity effects, biomass scale, and interaction-strength distributions as separately as possible.
Map physiological traits to response parameters with a sourced hierarchical model rather than unsourced beta classes.
Model drought events with duration and serial dependence, retain seasonality, publish seeds, and report ensemble distributions under common random numbers.
Give pollution and habitat distinct units, bounds, exposure pathways, calibration data, and factorial independent/joint scenarios.
Implement one equation-code contract with tests for sign, matrix orientation, update order, nonnegativity, and limiting cases.
Establish numerical convergence with step refinement and compare Euler, RK4, and a trusted adaptive solver on identical forcing.
Turn each viability recommendation into a decision analysis with intervention variables, ecological constraints, cost/resource tradeoffs, uncertainty, and larger-environment metrics.

results_trace.summary: precipitation-linked peak reading: high precipitation -> abundance peaks -> low precipitation -> low states. Boundary: Attach the exact time series and species legend to the interpretation.
competition-at-peak reading: high abundance -> stronger competition -> species separation. Boundary: This mechanism is encoded by the model and not independently observed.
mutualism-at-scarcity reading: scarce precipitation -> low stable states -> no modeled extinction. Boundary: Define extinction and verify positivity/clipping effects.
rapid-change warning result: abrupt precipitation transition -> sharp A/B/C decline -> management relevance. Boundary: Retain the manipulated input and avoid causal certainty beyond the model.
irregular-cycle contrast: month-18 precipitation reduction without abrupt transition -> stable A/B/C. Boundary: Clarify why reducing precipitation to one tenth is described as non-dramatic.
two-species benefit ranking: six pairs -> three positive/three negative -> ordered B values. Boundary: Preserve all pairs, units, horizon, and the pointwise baseline.
three-species benefit ranking: four triples -> three positive/one negative -> ordered B values. Boundary: Composition still matters; richness alone does not determine sign.
four-species maximum result: ABCD -> B=6.987 x 10^4 -> exceeds k=2/3 maxima. Boundary: State whether B is a time average, integral, endpoint, or another aggregation.

richness-positive-share conclusion: k increase -> positive-case proportion increase -> maximum benefit increase. Boundary: The result is exhaustive only for four selected species under one parameterization.
standard-type stability reading: large precipitation fluctuation -> bounded standard abundance. Boundary: Quantify the stability band and compare matched parameters.
sensitive-tolerant contrast: sensitive fluctuation vs tolerant drought persistence + wet decline. Boundary: The type coefficient and interaction pathway jointly generate the contrast.

type-benefit comparison: sensitive mean benefit > tolerant mean benefit; k increase -> sensitive benefit faster. Boundary: The printed table includes zero and negative cases that should remain visible.
mixed-composition result: one tolerant + three sensitive -> subset benefits -> close to tolerant case. Boundary: Define a distance metric before claiming little difference.
drought-regime benefit result: greater/less drought -> k=2/3 benefits -> similar rankings with level shifts. Boundary: Table 10's second row label must be reconciled before interpretation.
human-stressor contrast: pollution only vs habitat only vs both -> decline ordering. Boundary: The chosen schedules differ in scale, so effect magnitude is not intrinsically comparable.

rainfall recommendation: stable precipitation result -> artificial rainfall in dry months -> stability/diversity. Boundary: Water intervention feasibility, allocation, and unintended effects are not modeled.

richness-and-mixing recommendation: positive richness signal + complementary type weaknesses -> mixed planting. Boundary: Select species through controlled subset evidence and ecological compatibility.

pollution-habitat recommendation: lower emissions + improved environment + more habitat -> viability. Boundary: This direction is plausible, but costs and larger-environment effects are not quantified.
optimized-trajectory result: RK4 curve smoother + smaller declines -> claimed accuracy. Boundary: Compare numerical error against a converged reference, not visual smoothness alone.
result-stack close: population + benefit + scenarios + diagnostics -> strengths/weaknesses. Boundary: The quality close should distinguish achievement from untested scope.

task_reconstruction.decision: Treat all quantitative conclusions as conditional on the four-species parameterization, synthetic weather and factory schedules, undocumented calibration, and code inconsistencies; use the route as an inspectable scenario framework rather than a validated ecological forecast.

weaknesses.summary: Initial abundances 34, 34, 29, and 33 lack sampling area, date, observation protocol, uncertainty, and transfer rationale.
Capacities and growth ceilings are inferred qualitatively from drought adaptability and root length without a calibration objective or uncertainty.
The common alpha, S0, k_sigma, and k_i constants are said to come from fitting and empirical analysis, but no data, fit, residuals, or source mapping is shown.
Eq.1 has no explicit initial condition, calibrated r_i/N_i, equilibrium check, or observation unit for the ideal single-species baseline.
Eq.2 does not state whether the summation excludes j=i; Listings 1, 3, and 4 set the sigma diagonal to one, so including j=i in Eq.2 would double-count x_i/N_i.
Eq.3 assumes that all pair interactions switch linearly from competition to mutual benefit at drought threshold S0 without direct evidence or alternative forms.
Eq.4 yields S in [0,1] only when P lies in [0,Pmax]; Pmax's area, period, units, and clipping behavior are not specified.
The prose motivates Eq.5 by saying excessive rain can drown plants and slow growth, but the printed Logistic curve is monotone increasing toward L_i and cannot decline at high precipitation.
Listing 1 computes r_i=0.5L_i/(1+exp(kD_j)), whereas Eq.5 has L_i/(1+exp(-k_iP_j)); D is undefined, the factor 0.5 is new, the sign changes, and the forcing variable differs.
Eq.6 is called linearly positive without sourcing alpha_i or showing that capacity remains ecologically meaningful over all stress and extension scenarios.
Table 2 states alpha_i=0.6 and k_sigma=0.002, but Table 3 drops k_sigma and places 0.002 under alpha_i, changing a central parameter by a factor of 300 if read literally.
Eq.9-Eq.10 claim root-shoot-based directed matrices but provide no transformation from the cited measurements to 32 off-diagonal values or their uncertainty.
Eq.7 uses a pointwise maximum that may switch monoculture identity each month, creating a comparator trajectory that no single feasible monoculture necessarily follows.
Eq.8 defines time-varying B(t), while Tables 4-11 report one value described as an average at all times without a printed aggregation equation, horizon treatment, or uncertainty.
Species biomass weights B_i have no units, observation basis, or indication whether they are per individual, dry mass, unit-area biomass, or scaled coefficients.
The richness conclusion confounds species count, subset identity, pair parameters, initial total abundance, and biomass weights, and reports no stochastic uncertainty.
Assumption 5 says there are only sensitive and drought-tolerant types, but Section 4.2.2 introduces standard, sensitive, and drought-tolerant types.

Eq.11 assigns beta=0.5 to sensitive and beta=1.5 to drought-tolerant plants; for S>S0 the larger beta reduces N_i more strongly, which conflicts with the stated type interpretation unless another mapping is used.
Figures 5-10 use small, low-contrast legends and show no uncertainty, replicate spread, threshold, or quantitative stability annotation.
Listing 2 generates independent monthly precipitation amounts from a marginal histogram; it does not model drought-event frequency, duration, or serial persistence despite the scenario label.
The lesser-drought scenario swaps histogram bins 1-2 with 9-10 but supplies no meteorological rationale and does not explain how the swap changes drought frequency rather than only amounts.
All Monte Carlo panels omit random seeds, number of realizations, ensemble summaries, uncertainty bands, seasonality, and comparison with held-out precipitation.
Figure 12 is captioned as plant numbers in regular and irregular drought cycles even though it displays greater- and lesser-drought precipitation sequences.
Table 10 labels its second row drought-tolerant type instead of lesser drought, leaving the k=2 weather-scenario comparison ambiguous.
Claims that biomass is stable and high under both greater and lesser drought use no stability metric, threshold, uncertainty interval, or matched-random comparison.
Eq.12 adds S in [0,1] to an unscaled pollution degree PO and then substitutes T into formulas calibrated for S, so T can leave the declared domain.
Eq.13 omits time-step scaling, pollution units, the distribution of delta, calibration of mu_i, and a nonnegativity constraint later added only in code.
Eq.13 uses species-specific sum_i mu_i x_i, but Listing 4 implements one scalar mu times total abundance.
H is described as the impact or proportion of habitat reduction, but Eq.15 defines H=A/A0, the retained-habitat fraction; reversing this interpretation reverses the model effect.
Table 12's placement of delta in [0.02,0.06] does not unambiguously identify affected months, distribution, or realized monthly values.
Figure 16 is captioned effects of drought severity and frequency although its panels are pollution, habitat reduction, and their combination.
The sensitivity section does not state whether parameters are perturbed one at a time, by species, or jointly, whether random inputs are held fixed, or how Table 13 signs are computed.
The claim that all changes are within an acceptable range gives no acceptance threshold, decision tolerance, confidence interval, or global sensitivity coverage.
Figure 18's smoother and less-declining RK4 trajectory is called more accurate without a reference solution, step-refinement test, error norm, or observed population comparator.
Listing 3 again uses r_i=0.5L_i/(1+exp(-kS_j)), differing from both Eq.5 and Listing 1 in scale, sign, and forcing variable.
Listing 4 calculates r_i and sigma from the stored T_j before updating PO and overwriting T_j, while capacity uses the newly updated T_j; one step therefore mixes old and new stress states.
The printed RK4 route fixes an implicit one-month step and monthly forcing across stages but reports no convergence, stiffness, positivity, or code-versus-equation parity test.
The required T and rainfall.xlsx input, full MATLAB files, seeds, package/toolbox versions, and executable output reproduction are absent.
The paper calls one scenario comparison robust, reasonable, and accurate without external plant observations, calibration residuals, holdout data, or predictive error.

Artificial rainfall, mixed planting, emission reduction, and habitat expansion are directionally linked to results but lack feasibility, resource, cost, ecological compatibility, and larger-environment impact analysis.
The required impact on the larger environment is addressed qualitatively; no larger-environment state, metric, causal pathway, or quantified consequence appears in the model.
